items.stem: What compass bearing is due south-west?
items.markingKey: D. Bearings run clockwise from north: S = 180°, W = 270°, SW = 225°.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "A bearing of 090° means facing north." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Bearings are measured clockwise from north (000°), so 090° is due east.
items.markingKey: Bearings are measured clockwise from north (000°), so 090° is due east. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a 1:25 000 map shows more detail than a 1:250 000 map.
items.answer: It is a larger scale: 1 cm represents only 250 m rather than 2.5 km, so each area is drawn bigger and small features such as footpaths and buildings can be shown.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is a larger scale: 1 cm represents only 250 m rather than 2.5 km, so each area is drawn bigger and small features such as footpaths and buildings can be shown. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source A – Official report (paraphrased): Summary of the resolutions of the International Meridian Conference, Washington, D.C., October 1884

The delegates resolved that a single prime meridian should be adopted for all nations in place of the many then in use, and that it should pass through the centre of the transit instrument at the Observatory of Greenwich. France abstained and continued to use the Paris meridian on its own maps for some decades.

What is the message of Source A about map skills such as grid references, scale and direction? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: A single world prime meridian at Greenwich was agreed in 1884, although not every country accepted it at once.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How accurately do students at our school estimate walking distances compared with measurements from a 1:25 000 map?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Choose a route; measure it on a 1:25 000 map using string and the scale bar; survey 20 students for estimates; walk the route with a GPS app; compare results in a table and graph; evaluate measurement errors.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Choose a route; measure it on a 1:25 000 map using string and the scale bar; survey 20 students for estimates; walk the route with a GPS app; compare results in a table and graph; evaluate measurement errors. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "longitude".
items.answer: The angular distance of a place east or west of the prime meridian at Greenwich, measured from 0° to 180°

items.stem: Explain why lines of longitude are used to work out time differences.
items.answer: The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so the Sun appears to move 15° of longitude each hour; places further east see sunrise and noon earlier.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so the Sun appears to move 15° of longitude each hour; places further east see sunrise and noon earlier. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a large-scale map and a small-scale map.
items.answer: A large-scale map (e.g. 1:10 000) shows a small area in great detail; a small-scale map (e.g. 1:1 000 000) shows a large area with little detail.
items.markingKey: A large-scale map (e.g. 1:10 000) shows a small area in great detail; a small-scale map (e.g. 1:1 000 000) shows a large area with little detail. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mei writes: "Lines of longitude are all the same distance apart everywhere on Earth." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Lines of longitude converge at the poles: 1° of longitude is about 111 km at the equator but 0 km at the poles. Lines of latitude are (almost) evenly spaced.

items.stem: Explain why Arno Peters argued that the Mercator projection gave a biased view of the world.
items.answer: Mercator enlarges high-latitude regions such as Europe and North America and shrinks tropical regions, so Peters argued it made the Global North look more important than countries of the Global South.

items.answer: Mercator preserves shape and direction locally but exaggerates area towards the poles; Gall–Peters preserves relative area but stretches shapes, especially near the equator.

items.stem: In 2023 the Netherlands had an estimated population of 17,900,000 and an area of 41,850 km². Calculate its population density.
items.answer: 428 people per km²
items.markingKey: Density = population ÷ area (M1) = 17,900,000 ÷ 41,850 = 428 people per km² (A1). Units required.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Equal-area projections should replace the Mercator projection in all classrooms."
items.answer: Thesis: Partly agree: equal-area maps are better for comparing areas, but the strongest approach is to use several projections and teach what each distorts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they show the true relative size of countries; they reduce a Eurocentric impression of the world. Counter-arguments: shapes are distorted, so countries look stretched; no single projection is best for every purpose; students should learn to compare them. The angular distance of a place east or west of the prime meridian at Greenwich, measured from 0° to 180°
A method of representing the curved surface of the Earth on a flat map, which always distorts area, shape, distance or direction

items.answer: On a Mercator map a line of constant compass bearing (a rhumb line) is straight, so a navigator could draw a straight line between ports and follow one bearing.

items.stem: Using John Snow's 1854 cholera map of Soho, London as an example, explain spatial analysis, the core idea of GIS.
items.answer: Snow plotted deaths as bars on a street map and found they clustered around the Broad Street water pump; the pump handle was removed. Layering disease cases with the location of water sources revealed a pattern and a cause.

items.stem: Global smartphone users went from 1,100 million in 2012 to 6,400 million in 2022. Which is the percentage change?

items.answer: Origin: Summary of INPE information about its PRODES and DETER monitoring systems. Purpose: to explain and publicise how a government agency monitors deforestation. Value: It comes from the agency that runs the systems, so the description of how they work is authoritative. Limitation: As a government source it may stress successes and say little about cloud cover, enforcement failures or political pressure on the figures.

items.stem: Los Angeles lies at about 118°W and Cairo at about 31°E. Using local solar time (the Sun crosses 15° of longitude per hour), if it is 10:00 local solar time in Los Angeles, what is the local solar time in Cairo?
items.answer: 19:56 (Cairo is 9 h 56 min ahead)
items.markingKey: Longitude difference 149° (M1); ÷ 15 = 9.93 h = 9 h 56 min (A1); Cairo is east so ahead → 19:56 (A1). Official time zones differ from solar time.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How does the choice of map projection affect students' estimates of the size of African countries?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Prepare two world maps (Mercator, Gall–Peters); ask two groups to estimate Africa's size relative to Greenland and Europe; record results; compare with real areas from an atlas; present in a bar chart; evaluate sample size.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Prepare two world maps (Mercator, Gall–Peters); ask two groups to estimate Africa's size relative to Greenland and Europe; record results; compare with real areas from an atlas; present in a bar chart; evaluate sample size. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How has the area of green space in our city changed between 2005 and 2025, according to satellite images on Google Earth?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Choose a study area; use Google Earth historical imagery for 2005, 2015 and 2025; trace green spaces; measure areas with a grid or GIS tool; record in a table; calculate % change; interview a council planner; evaluate image resolution.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Choose a study area; use Google Earth historical imagery for 2005, 2015 and 2025; trace green spaces; measure areas with a grid or GIS tool; record in a table; calculate % change; interview a council planner; evaluate image resolution. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Lukas is investigating map skills such as grid references, scale and direction and proposes the research question: "What are maps?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a closed, very broad definition question with no place, group or measurable focus Improved: "How accurately do students at our school estimate walking distances compared with measurements from a 1:25 000 map?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a closed, very broad definition question with no place, group or measurable focus); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How accurately do students at our school estimate walking distances compared with measurements from a 1:25 000 map?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Book extract (paraphrased): Paraphrase of arguments made by Arno Peters, a German historian, in "The New Cartography" (1983)

The familiar world map greatly overstates the size of the countries of the North, which were mainly colonial powers, and understates the size of the countries of Africa, Asia and Latin America. A map that shows every country in its true proportion of area is needed for a fairer picture of the world.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into map types and map projections, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of arguments made by Arno Peters, a German historian, in "The New Cartography" (1983). Purpose: to persuade readers that the Mercator projection is biased and that his own equal-area projection should replace it. Value: It clearly shows the perspective of the main promoter of the Gall–Peters projection and the political argument behind it. Limitation: Peters was promoting his own map, so he does not mention that equal-area maps also distort shape or that earlier cartographers had designed similar projections.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Geospatial technology has done more good than harm."
items.answer: Thesis: Mostly agree: the benefits for planning and safety are large, but they depend on rules that protect privacy and on fair access to data.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: GIS and satellites support disaster response, planning and monitoring of forests and ice; GPS improves navigation, farming and emergency services. Counter-arguments: location tracking threatens privacy; access to data and skills is unequal between countries. Thesis/conclusion: Mostly agree: the benefits for planning and safety are large, but they depend on rules that protect privacy and on fair access to data. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: On a 1:50,000 Ordnance Survey-style map, grid lines are 2 cm apart. A lake covers about 4 grid squares. Estimate the area of the lake in km² and explain your method.
items.answer: about 4 km²
items.markingKey: 2 cm × 50,000 = 100,000 cm = 1 km, so each grid square is 1 km × 1 km = 1 km² (M1 R1); 4 squares ≈ 4 km² (A1). Partly-filled squares counted as halves.

A map that shows every country in its true proportion of area is needed for a fairer picture of the world.

"Equal-area projections should replace the Mercator projection in all classrooms." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Partly agree: equal-area maps are better for comparing areas, but the strongest approach is to use several projections and teach what each distorts.
items.markingKey: From the source: Mercator maps exaggerate the size of the Global North, so an equal-area map gives a fairer view of the world. Own knowledge for: they show the true relative size of countries; they reduce a Eurocentric impression of the world. Own knowledge against: shapes are distorted, so countries look stretched; no single projection is best for every purpose; students should learn to compare them. Judgement: Partly agree: equal-area maps are better for comparing areas, but the strongest approach is to use several projections and teach what each distorts. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The angular distance of a place north or south of the equator, measured in degrees from 0° to 90°"?
items.answer: latitude
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of latitude.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "topographic map".
items.answer: A detailed map showing relief (with contour lines) and physical and human features of an area
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a detailed map showing relief (with contour lines) and physical and human features of an area. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "crowd-sourced mapping"?
options: The angular distance of a place north or south of the equator, measured in degrees from 0° to 90°
A US satellite navigation system in which receivers calculate their position from the signals of at least four satellites
A projection, such as the Gall–Peters, that shows the relative sizes of land masses correctly but distorts their shapes
Creating maps from data contributed by many volunteers, as in OpenStreetMap
items.answer: Creating maps from data contributed by many volunteers, as in OpenStreetMap
items.markingKey: D. "crowd-sourced mapping" is creating maps from data contributed by many volunteers, as in OpenStreetMap.

items.stem: Explain why eastings are always given before northings in a grid reference.
items.answer: It is an agreed convention: if everyone reads along (east) first and then up (north), each grid reference identifies only one square, so map users cannot confuse two different locations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is an agreed convention: if everyone reads along (east) first and then up (north), each grid reference identifies only one square, so map users cannot confuse two different locations. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why every flat world map distorts the Earth in some way.
items.answer: The Earth is a sphere (a curved surface); it cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing, so a projection must give up accuracy in area, shape, distance or direction.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Earth is a sphere (a curved surface); it cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing, so a projection must give up accuracy in area, shape, distance or direction. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "GPS works by the phone sending a signal up to the satellites." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: GPS receivers only receive: they compare timing signals from several satellites to calculate their position. The satellites do not know where the user is.
items.markingKey: GPS receivers only receive: they compare timing signals from several satellites to calculate their position. The satellites do not know where the user is. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a six-figure grid reference is more useful than a four-figure grid reference for locating a building.
items.answer: A four-figure reference only identifies a 1 km square; a six-figure reference divides the square into tenths in each direction and locates a point to within about 100 m.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A four-figure reference only identifies a 1 km square; a six-figure reference divides the square into tenths in each direction and locates a point to within about 100 m. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Arjun writes: "Greenland is bigger than Africa, as a world map clearly shows." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: That impression comes from the Mercator projection; Africa is about 14 times larger in area.
items.markingKey: That impression comes from the Mercator projection; Africa is about 14 times larger in area. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why crowd-sourced maps were important after the 2010 Haiti earthquake.
items.answer: Official maps of Port-au-Prince were poor; volunteers traced roads and buildings from satellite images in OpenStreetMap within days, giving responders up-to-date maps of damage and access routes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Official maps of Port-au-Prince were poor; volunteers traced roads and buildings from satellite images in OpenStreetMap within days, giving responders up-to-date maps of damage and access routes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why "How accurately do students at our school estimate walking distances compared with measurements from a 1:25 000 map?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into map skills such as grid references, scale and direction.
items.answer: It practises scale and distance skills, links to the related concept of scale and produces data the student can collect first-hand.
items.markingKey: It practises scale and distance skills, links to the related concept of scale and produces data the student can collect first-hand. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Boston Public Schools' decision in 2017 shows how map choice affects understanding.
items.answer: The district began using Gall–Peters maps alongside Mercator maps in social studies classrooms. Students could compare projections and see that Africa and South America are much larger than Mercator suggests.
items.markingKey: Context (The district began using Gall–Peters maps alongside Mercator maps in social studies classrooms.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: students could compare projections and see that Africa and South America are much larger than Mercator suggests. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how map choice affects understanding.

items.stem: Write one well-structured paragraph (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) in answer to this question: Explain why GIS is useful for planning responses to floods.
items.answer: GIS can overlay layers such as river levels, elevation, housing and roads, so planners can see which homes and routes are at risk and plan evacuation and defences.
items.markingKey: Content: GIS can overlay layers such as river levels, elevation, housing and roads, so planners can see which homes and routes are at risk and plan evacuation and defences. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Two places lie on the same line of longitude, one at 55°S and the other at 30°S. Given that 1° of latitude is about 111 km, estimate the distance between them.
items.answer: about 2,775 km
items.markingKey: Difference in latitude = 25° (crossing the equator adds both values) (M1); × 111 km = 2,775 km (A1).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the International Meridian Conference of 1884 in Washington, D.C. shows why map conventions are agreed internationally.
items.answer: Delegates from 25 nations voted to adopt Greenwich as the prime meridian (0°) for the world. A single reference line for longitude allowed consistent navigation charts and, later, standard time zones.
items.markingKey: Context (Delegates from 25 nations voted to adopt Greenwich as the prime meridian (0°) for the world.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: 2023 estimates: the United Kingdom – population 68,300,000, area 243,610 km²; Singapore – population 5,900,000, area 735 km². Calculate the population density of each country and state how many times more densely populated Singapore is than the United Kingdom.
items.answer: the United Kingdom: 280.4 /km²; Singapore: 8,027.2 /km²; Singapore is about 28.6 times as dense.
items.markingKey: M1 density = population ÷ area for each; A1 280.4; A1 8,027.2; A1 ratio 28.6 (allow ±0.2). A high national density can hide very uneven distribution.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Digital maps on phones have made traditional map-reading skills unnecessary."
items.answer: Thesis: Largely false: digital tools are powerful but depend on power and signal, and map-reading builds spatial understanding that users need to interpret and check digital maps.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: GPS gives instant location and turn-by-turn directions; digital maps update quickly and can show live data such as traffic.
